newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD casts doubt on government's tax reform offer.
newsitem.headline: SPD casts doubt on government's tax reform offer.

text.p: The parliamentary leader of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Friday cast doubts on the government's willingness to cooperate with the SPD on a major tax reform.

Rudolf Scharping said during a parliamentary debate that as long as Chancellor Helmut Kohl was bashing the SPD around the country as a party of "liars and hypocrites", there was little chance Kohl could count on SPD support for tax reform.

"You will not find us willing to be your partner in here if you are out there in the country criticising us," Scharping said, referring to the chancellor's attacks on the SPD during a recent party gathering in the state of Hesse.
The SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, has used its majority in the Bundesrat to thwart numerous government initiatives and has the power to derail Kohl's tax reform.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday formally accepted an SPD offer to work towards cutting the taxes in 1998, a year earlier than the government's plan.
But Waigel hedged this with stiff conditions that the SPD said were unlikely to be fulfilled. Waigel said tax reform could be passed by August and implemented in January.
For this he demanded the opposition accept his plan as the basis for negotiation and pledge not to use its majority in the upper house of parliament to force through a compromise.

"We are prepared to launch the tax reform already on January 1, 1998, but you must be willing to take our suggestions as a basis for negotiations and work together constructively with us in the Bundesrat," Waigel said.
SPD spokeswoman Mechthild Wiebusch said there was little chance the SPD would agree to negotiate on Waigel's terms. She said it was up to the government to work with the SPD on a new plan.
"It is not up to us," Wiebusch said. "It depends on what the government does next. We are ready to talk at any hour of any day."
Lafontaine earlier threatened to block the government's tax cutting reform measures in the Bundesrat in its current form because it would not bring real tax relief to most workers.
He also said the SPD would oppose an increase in the value-added tax (VAT) to finance the income tax cuts.

Waigel said he hoped the SPD offer to advance the date of the reform was serious and not just a cheap tactical trick. He said time was pressing and the SPD would have to refrain from sending the bill to conference committee.
Waigel said the bill needed to be completed by August at the latest if it is going to take effect next January, rather than at the start of 1999 as the government has proposed.

"Everything else would be a cheap offer made without believing in it ever being realised," Waigel said. "You have to say farewell to your blockade tactics if you are willing to work with us constructively."
